name: Core stability (plank, dead bug)
lead: Core stability is a person's ability to control the position and movement of the trunk, meaning the muscles around the spine, pelvis and abdomen. [1] The plank, an isometric hold resembling a push-up position, and the dead bug, a lying limb-movement drill, are two of the most common exercises used to train it. [1][2] People in posture and looksmaxxing communities use them to build a stronger trunk, with the aim of standing taller and more upright, correcting anterior pelvic tilt and showing a firmer, leaner-looking midsection. [3]

Sports-medicine reviews describe the core as the group of trunk muscles surrounding the spine and abdominal viscera, working together with gluteal, hip and paraspinal muscles to stabilise the spine and pelvis. [4] Core strengthening is used in sport and as a therapeutic exercise for low back pain. [4][6] Wikipedia lists planks, side planks and dead bugs among exercises suggested for anterior pelvic tilt, while noting that the sourcing for that section is weak. [3]

Research on the core stability model is mixed. A 2010 critical review re-examined its original findings and principles,[5] and Wikipedia states that core-specific training has not been shown to beat general exercise for injury prevention or performance, at best matching general non-specific exercise.[1] A 2023 meta-analysis of 21 trials in healthy people found core training improved balance outcomes, and also examined throwing and jumping.[7] No published study has tested plank or dead bug training for pelvic tilt or visual appearance.

paras: The core muscles listed in encyclopedic sources include the pelvic floor, transversus abdominis, multifidus, internal and external obliques, rectus abdominis, erector spinae and diaphragm. Breathing can influence core posture and movement. [1]

The plank is also called a front hold or abdominal bridge. A forearm plank rests the body on the forearms and toes; variants include the side plank, reverse plank and extended plank. Primary muscles for the front plank are given as the erector spinae, rectus abdominis and transversus abdominis, with the shoulder girdle, glutes and legs as secondary. The side plank emphasises the obliques, transversus abdominis and hip abductors. [2]

Wikipedia describes core stability as a person's ability to stabilise the non-limb parts of the body, controlling tone, position and movement of the trunk. It notes that breathing, especially diaphragm use, can influence core posture, and that some researchers think deeper breathing raises intra-abdominal pressure, which supports the lumbar spine.[1]

The dead bug is performed lying on the back with arms and knees raised, lowering opposite arm and leg while the lower back stays controlled against the floor. The bird dog, a related drill on hands and knees, appears with it in many programs.[9]

Wikipedia lists the forearm plank, side plank, reverse plank, extended plank and medicine-ball variants. Isometric plank holds are common in Pilates, yoga (where the position appears as Chaturanga Dandasana) and training for boxing and other sports.[2] Guinness World Records entries cited by Wikipedia include a front elbow plank of 9 hours 38 minutes 47 seconds by Josef Salek in May 2023, which followed Daniel Scali's 9 hours 30 minutes in 2021.[2] Such feats are novelties; most lifters treat planks as brief trunk-endurance sets.

sections.h: How it is meant to improve appearance
paras: Posture programs list planks, side planks and dead bugs alongside glute bridges and hip thrusts as measures for anterior pelvic tilt, the forward rotation of the pelvis that exaggerates the lower-back curve and pushes the abdomen outward.[3] The chain proponents describe is a stronger trunk, better pelvic control, a more upright stance and a firmer-looking midsection. Wikipedia's pelvic tilt article notes the sourcing for its exercise section is weak.[3]
Others use these drills as support work for heavy lifting, where a braced trunk helps keep the spine in position during squats and deadlifts and so supports training that builds the physique.[9]

Planks, side planks and dead bugs appear in posture programs alongside glute bridges and hip thrusts as anterior pelvic tilt measures. [3] Proponents link a stronger trunk with better posture and a leaner-looking midsection.

On T Nation, one lifter's suggested quick routine for trunk work lists kettlebell plank transfers, dead bugs and weighted back extensions, framed around back and lifting health rather than appearance. [9]

sections.h: Origins of the core stability approach
paras: Core stability training grew in rehabilitation and sports medicine in the late twentieth century as a way to treat low back pain and prevent injuries, and is now widespread. A 2008 Current Sports Medicine Reports review summarised the anatomy and how strengthening is progressed, and a 2006 review in Sports Medicine discussed the role of core stability in athletic function.[4][8]

Stuart McGill, Distinguished Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo, is widely associated with trunk-stability exercises for back health; the exercises commonly called the McGill Big 3 (curl-up, side bridge and bird dog) appear in the infobox here, though the Wikipedia page for McGill does not itself describe them.[12] Critics such as Lederman, in a 2010 review, argue spinal stabilisation principles should be re-examined against broader knowledge of motor control.[5]

A review in Current Sports Medicine Reports summarises the anatomy of the core, how core strengthening is progressed, and the evidence for its efficacy in musculoskeletal conditions. [4] Another review discusses the role of core stability in athletic function. [8] A critical 2010 review argues that the principles of spinal stabilisation approaches should be re-examined against wider knowledge of motor control. [5]

Wikipedia reports that trunk-specific exercise has not been shown to prevent sports injuries or improve sports performance. [1] A review of 270 trials in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, cited by Wikipedia, found isometric exercises including planks and wall sits were more effective than other exercise types for lowering blood pressure. [2] That finding concerns blood pressure, not posture or appearance.

Wikipedia also records that it is commonly believed that insufficient core stability causes low back pain and lower-limb injuries, and that cited systematic reviews find stabilisation exercise for low back pain gives results similar to general exercise.[1]
No trial has tested plank or dead bug training for pelvic tilt or visual appearance. Trials and reviews of core stability training in other settings are described below.

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis in Biology of Sport included 22 studies (21 in the meta-analysis) of core training programs of at least four weeks in healthy people over 12, and reported that core training improved balance outcomes; it also examined throwing, hitting and jumping and compared isolated with combined core training.[7]

A review in the Journal of Athletic Training, summarising a meta-analysis of randomised trials in adults with chronic low back pain, compared core stability exercise with general exercise on pain, function, quality of life and absenteeism.[6] A 2021 review examined core stability in non-specific chronic low back pain,[10] and a 2020 randomised controlled trial in Japan tested core stability plus hip exercises in people with non-specific low back pain and reported improved physical function and activity.[11] Trials in children with cerebral palsy and Down syndrome have also tested core stabilisation exercise on balance.[13][14]

card.summary: Plank and dead bug trunk drills pitched for posture and pelvic tilt; broader core-stability research shows modest benefit over general exercise.
card.note: Wikipedia notes limited research support for the core stability model.

quick.overview:
Core stability training uses holds like the plank and controlled movements like the dead bug to train the trunk. Posture communities include it in pelvic tilt routines.

Encyclopedic sources say research support for the core stability model is limited, and nothing found tests it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: The exercises train the abdominal, back and hip muscles to hold the spine and pelvis in position under load or movement.
quick.risks: Generally low risk. Back pain during exercise is usually referred to a clinician.

chain: Plank and dead bug train the abdominal, back and hip muscles
A stronger trunk holds the pelvis and spine in position
More upright posture and a firmer-looking midsection
angle.text: Practitioners use planks and dead bugs to strengthen the muscles that hold the pelvis and spine in place, hoping to improve standing posture and reduce anterior pelvic tilt. Many also train the same muscles to build a more defined, tighter-looking waist and abdomen. Whether this changes visible pelvic tilt has not been tested directly.
